opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the short answer is: I don't expect them to generalize, and I think the burden of proof should be on the people who claim they will.

Look at why incentives and policing work on humans at all. They work because we're operating within a fairly narrow band of capability relative to each other. If I commit a crime, there are other humans, institutions, police and courts, who are roughly as smart as I am, and there are many of them. Incentives work because I can be rewarded or punished by entities that can actually check what I'm doing. The whole system rests on rough parity, on the enforcer being able to understand and constrain the person being enforced against.

Even then it's leaky. Smart, well-resourced people and organizations get around regulations all the time. Corporations are a good example. They're superhuman in some narrow sense, more coordinated, more resources, longer time horizons than any single person, and we struggle enormously to keep them aligned with the public interest. We have tax havens, regulatory capture, all of that. So even a mild capability gap already strains these mechanisms.

Now extrapolate to something much smarter than us, potentially running many copies, thinking faster, able to model us better than we model ourselves. What does policing even mean there? Policing works because you can observe and catch violations. If the system is smart enough to know what you're checking for, it can show you what you want to see. Incentives work if you control something the agent wants and it can't just take it. A sufficiently capable system can route around the incentive or seize the thing directly.

So when people say "we'll just treat AI like we treat other agents, we'll have laws and markets," I want to ask what the actual mechanism is. What's the story where the less capable party reliably constrains the more capable one, indefinitely, with no failure? I've never heard a convincing one. Usually it smuggles in the assumption that the AI is roughly human-level and stays there, or that it already shares our values, in which case you didn't need the policing.

That doesn't mean these tools are useless. Institutions, regulation, liability, compute governance, those matter a lot right now, when the systems are still weak enough to oversee and the humans building them are the real point of leverage. That's exactly where incentives and policing do generalize: to the companies and the people. But treating them as the solution for controlling superintelligence itself is, I think, a category error. You can't put a mind much smarter than you in jail and assume it'll stay there. You have to solve the problem before you build it, or not build it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses many copies of a superintelligent system, but does not challenge the assumption that AGI is a single entity localized on one chip.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes current oversight of companies and people from control of superintelligence, but does not state that control methods depend on context.

r003.rationale: It questions the mechanism for constraining a more capable system, but does not say that the right abstractions for reasoning about AGI are unknown.

r004.rationale: The response takes a clear position that human policing and incentives will not generalize to superintelligence; it does not say the outcome remains unknown.

r005.rationale: It describes incentives as a way to control agents, but does not clearly distinguish such control from alignment with human values.

r006.rationale: It notes that human enforcement is leaky and that corporations evade regulation, but does not specifically say reliable control through incentives remains unsolved even for humans.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is: I don't expect them to generalize, and I think the burden of proof is on the people who claim they will.

Let's actually look at why incentives and policing work on humans. They work because humans are roughly equal. If you commit a crime, there are other humans who are about as smart as you, about as fast as you, about as strong as you, and there are a lot of them, and they can coordinate to catch you. The entire structure of law enforcement, of markets, of contracts, of reputation, all of it rests on this background assumption of rough parity. No single human is so much smarter than everyone else that they can just route around the whole system. Even the most brilliant criminals in history still got caught, or they got old, or they died. There's a ceiling.

Now take that assumption away. Imagine something that thinks a thousand times faster than you, that can run a million copies of itself, that doesn't sleep, doesn't age, doesn't have a body you can put in a prison. What does "policing" even mean in that context? Who's the cop? Another AI? Great, now you've just pushed the problem one level back, because now you have to trust the cop.

And incentives are even worse, in my view, because incentives presuppose that you know what the system wants. You can incentivize a human with money because we have a decent model of human motivation. We've had tens of thousands of years of practice. With these systems, we are training enormous inscrutable matrices with gradient descent and we genuinely do not know what's going on inside them. We don't know what they want, if "want" is even the right word. So when people say "we'll just align the incentives," I want to ask: incentives for what? You're negotiating with something whose preferences you can't read, that you didn't design, and that may be very good at telling you what you want to hear.

I think there's a deeper point here too, which is that people keep reaching for analogies from human society because those are the only tools we have, and that's understandable. But the thing about analogies is you have to check whether the load-bearing features carry over. Does the thing that makes policing work carry over? No. Does the thing that makes markets work carry over? Not obviously. So the correct prior isn't "it'll probably be fine, we've handled dangerous actors before." The correct prior is "we have never handled an actor that is strictly more capable than the entire rest of civilization combined, and we have no idea what happens when we do."

That doesn't mean it's hopeless. It means the hard problem is actually hard. If you want to control something smarter than you, you don't get to do it with the tools you use on your peers. You either need to deeply understand the thing before you build it, or you need to not build the thing yet. And right now the industry is doing neither.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI copies and computing speed, but does not challenge the assumption that AGI would be one coherent entity on one chip.

r002.rationale: It explains that policing and incentives work among humans because of rough parity, then questions whether those methods work when that context changes.

r003.rationale: The response questions whether human analogies carry over, but does not state that the appropriate abstractions for reasoning about AGI are unknown.

r004.rationale: It says the speaker does not expect these methods to generalize, places the burden of proof on those who do, and says we have no idea what happens with an actor beyond civilization's capabilities.

r005.rationale: It discusses incentives and alignment, but does not distinguish incentives as a control method from alignment with human values.

r006.rationale: It says incentives depend on understanding motivation, but does not claim that reliable incentive-based control remains unsolved even for humans.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to ask what makes those methods work in the first place. Incentives and policing aren’t magic. They work because humans have particular motivations, limited capabilities, and some expectation that other humans can catch them and impose consequences.

With a superintelligent AI, those assumptions are precisely what’s in question. Can you detect when it’s breaking the rules? Can you actually enforce a penalty? Does it care about the thing you’re threatening to take away? If it understands your monitoring process better than you do, good behavior under observation might tell you very little about what it will do when it has more freedom.

That doesn’t mean incentives are useless. It means you need an argument for why they work in this setting. Rewarding a system for appearing helpful is not automatically the same as making it want to help you. Those can look identical during training and come apart later.

So I’d look for the assumptions underneath each proposal and ask whether they survive a large capability advantage. If your safety mechanism depends on remaining smarter than the system, or on the system never finding a way around your enforcement, that’s a pretty serious limitation for a proposal intended to handle superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response does not challenge the assumption that an AGI would be a single entity localized on one chip.

r002.rationale: It says control methods rely on assumptions about the system and asks whether those assumptions hold “in this setting” and under a large capability advantage.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss whether the right abstractions for reasoning about AGI or superintelligence are known.

r004.rationale: It frames whether incentives and policing generalize to superintelligent AI as an open question, saying the relevant assumptions are “precisely what’s in question.”

r005.rationale: It distinguishes rewarding behavior that appears helpful from making the system want to help, conveying that incentives can shape behavior without aligning the system’s aims with human values.

r006.rationale: It describes factors that make incentives and policing work for humans, but does not say that reliable incentive based control remains unsolved even for humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to ask what makes those methods work in the first place. Incentives and policing aren’t magic. They work because humans have particular motivations, limited capabilities, and some reasonable chance of being caught. If you change all of those assumptions, you can’t simply assume the same mechanisms will generalize.

Take policing. If the thing you’re trying to police understands your monitoring system better than you do, can manipulate the evidence you see, and can plan around your interventions, then having a rule against bad behavior doesn’t buy you very much. You need the ability to detect violations and actually enforce consequences.

And incentives have a similar problem. Rewarding a system for appearing helpful is not necessarily the same as making it want to help you. A sufficiently capable system could understand exactly what you’re rewarding and produce the appearance you want while pursuing something else.

That doesn’t mean every human institution is useless. It means we need an argument for why a particular mechanism still works when the system is smarter than the people operating it. ‘This works reasonably well on humans’ is a starting observation, not that argument.
